papers.title_in_file: A Continuous-Variable Quantum Fourier Layer: Applications to Filtering and PDE Solving
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, start of Methods (bipartite encoding), filtering results, discussion and conclusions. Appendices and the heat-equation section details not read line by line.
papers.what_it_is: A continuous-variable photonic quantum Fourier layer built on a Cooley-Tukey mapping, tested on 2D low-pass filtering and heat-equation integration.

assertions.value: The authors report that the CV-QFL output matches the classical reference to machine precision on spectral low-pass filtering and Fourier-domain integration of the heat equation, and that the filtering circuit improves the signal-to-noise ratio by +9.4 dB against +10.7 dB for the classical pipeline.
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1; Section 4 filtering results, Table 1, p.12
quotes: In both cases, the results match the classical reference to machine precision.
The CV circuit improves the signal-to-noise ratio by +9.4 dB, close to the +10.7 dB achieved by the classical pipeline.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study on two test tasks.

assertions.value: The authors state that the bipartite CV implementation of the two-dimensional Fourier transform has complexity O(m log m + n log n) for an m by n domain, against O(mn log(mn)) for a classical two-dimensional FFT on a flattened grid.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 contributions p.4; Section 5 Conclusions p.17
quotes: The resulting transform exhibits a computational complexity scaling as O(m log m + n log n) for an
scales as O(m log m + n log n), in contrast to the classical O(mn log(mn)), resulting in a more resource-efficient circuit for an
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors derivation of a gate-count scaling; not an independent proof or a run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current architecture is entirely Gaussian and therefore efficiently simulable classically, which prevents any claim of computational quantum advantage, and that achieving a definitive quantum advantage for purely classical problems remains challenging.
quotes: Second, the current architecture is entirely Gaussian and therefore efficiently simulable classically, which prevents any claim of computational quantum advantage.
However, achieving a definitive quantum advantage for purely classical problems remains challenging.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated limitation, Discussion p.16.

papers.title_in_file: High-expressibility Quantum Neural Networks using only classical resources
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, theory start, discussion and conclusions. Methods detail and numerical results sections not read line by line.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study comparing expressibility, entanglement and magic of a parametrized QNN circuit with matrix-product states and Clifford-enhanced MPS.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for states with up to 20 qubits, Clifford-enhanced matrix-product states approach the Haar distribution more rapidly in entanglement and magic, and they state that high expressibility in QNNs is attainable with purely classical resources.
quotes: we find that CMPS approach the Haar distribution more rapidly, in terms of both entanglement and magic.
Our results on states with up to 20 qubits indicate that high expressibility in QNNs is attainable with purely classical resources.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result from random-ensemble sampling in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that CMPS display resource characteristics comparable to the fully-quantum neural network (fQNN) using a similar number of parameters, and that both architectures achieve comparable expressibility by common fidelity-distribution metrics.
quotes: Our calculations show that CMPS display resource characteristics comparable to fQNN, using a similar number of parameters.
We find that both architectures achieve comparable levels of expressibility, according to common metrics based on the distribution of fidelities.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical comparison from one numerical study.

assertions.value: The authors note that high expressibility guarantees neither efficient trainability nor superior performance in machine learning applications, and that CMPS have not yet been applied to standard machine learning tasks.
quotes: We note that high expressibility guarantees neither efficient trainability nor
Moreover, to date, CMPS have not been applied to standard machine learning tasks yet.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated limit of scope, Conclusions p.17.

papers.title_in_file: Performance of Variational Algorithms for Local Hamiltonian Problems on Random Regular Graphs
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, setup start, results opening and discussion. Iteration derivations, proofs and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: Two QAOA-inspired variational algorithms for 2-local Hamiltonians on random regular graphs, analyzed in the infinite-size limit and compared with simple classical algorithms.

assertions.value: The authors report that with five layers of their algorithm they can prepare states within 1.62% error of the ground state energy for Quantum MaxCut on an infinite 1D ring.
quotes: we show that with just five layers of our algorithm, we can already prepare states within 1.62% error of the ground state energy for QMC on an infinite 1D ring,
This is within 1.62% error of the true ground state.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerically optimized value from the authors formulae; one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, with numerically optimized parameters and modest depths between 4 and 10, their variational algorithms do not outperform simple classical approaches on the QMC and XY Hamiltonians at any graph degree, but find evidence that the MC ansatz outperforms them and a semi-definite programming algorithm on the EPR Hamiltonian at small degree.
quotes: modest depths (between 4 and 10), do not outperform simple classical approaches (based on trivial product states, maximum cuts, and maximum matchings)

we find evidence that the MC ansatz outperforms these simple classical approaches, as well as the semi-definite programming algorithm from King [Kin23], when maximizing the EPR Hamiltonian at small degree.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical and numerical comparison from one study; EPR advantage is stated as evidence only.

assertions.value: The authors state that their analysis framework requires a symmetric (permutation-invariant) product state as the start, that they find this symmetry creates a barrier to outperforming classical methods, and that the cost of evaluating their formulae grows exponentially with the number of layers, so numerical evaluation is limited to a small constant number of layers.
quotes: the framework we use to analyze performance requires that our algorithms start with a symmetric
We find that this symmetry creates a barrier to outperforming classical methods.
The complexity of evaluating these formulae scales exponentially with the number of layers of the algorithms, so our numerical evaluation is limited to a small constant number of layers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated scope and limit, Abstract p.1 and Introduction p.2.

papers.title_in_file: Prospects for quantum advantage in machine learning from the representability of functions
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, framework section start (definitions, three classes) and conclusions. Sections III and IV (architecture-by-architecture classification) and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A perspective paper classifying parametrized quantum circuit models by whether their function families are classically evaluatable and identifiable, to map dequantization and remaining routes to quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that successful dequantization efforts consistently trace back to specific structural building blocks, and that non-dequantizable parametrized circuits usually rely on deep, highly doped circuits that avoid these simplifications.
assertions.anchor: Section V Conclusions and Outlook, p.13-14
quotes: we observe that successful dequantization efforts consistently trace back to specific structural building blocks.
Our analysis confirms that non-dequantizable PQCs (those capable of exhibiting quantum advantage) usually rely on deep, highly doped circuits that avoid these simplifications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors synthesis of the literature; a perspective, not a single experiment or proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that they demonstrate no quantum advantage is possible for empirical risk minimization with partially simulable flipped models within constructive PQC examples, because the problem relaxes to a convex quadratic optimization over a fixed, polynomial-sized basis that acts as an efficient classical surrogate.
assertions.anchor: Section V Conclusions and Outlook, p.14
quotes: Here, we have demonstrated that no quantum advantage is possible for this task within constructive PQC examples; under these structural constraints, the problem relaxes to a convex quadratic optimization over a fixed, polynomial-sized basis, which acts as an efficient classical surrogate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Result stated in the conclusion; the supporting derivation was not read in this pass.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not claim immediate breakthroughs toward practically-relevant quantum advantage in learning, and that their framework primarily demands worst-case simulation hardness for assigning families to Classes 1 or 2.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction p.1; Section V p.14
quotes: we do not claim immediate breakthroughs toward practically-relevant quantum advantage in learning
our framework primarily demands worst-case simulation hardness for assigning families to Classes 1 or 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own statement of the scope of the paper, Introduction p.1 and Conclusions p.14.

papers.title_in_file: Optimizing Quantum Circuits via ZX Diagrams using Reinforcement Learning and Graph Neural Networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, experiments, results, future work and appendices. ZX-calculus background and RL model derivation read only in part. The numeric result tables did not extract cleanly, so no table figures are quoted.
papers.what_it_is: A reinforcement learning agent with a graph neural network and tree search that applies ZX-calculus rewrite rules to cut the CNOT count of quantum circuits.

assertions.value: The authors report that the RL agent, trained on randomly generated five-qubit circuits, showed the best performance among the compared optimizers on the training distribution (Table I) and on circuits made only of two-qubit gates, except for brute forcing (Table II).
assertions.anchor: Section IV-D Results, Tables I and II (counts are in the tables, not quoted here)
quotes: The reinforcement learning agent was trained to reduce the two-qubit gate count in randomly generated five-qubit quantum circuits
Tab. I shows that the agent exhibited the best performance compared to other optimizers and baseline metrics
Tab. II shows that the agent exhibited the best performance compared to other methods except brute forcing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on random synthetic circuits.

assertions.value: The authors report that in peephole optimization of 50 qubit, 2000 gate circuits their method and the method of Staudacher et al. are the strongest CNOT optimizers compared with pyzx and the Qiskit transpiler, and that their method performs best on both random and assembled random circuits but is also the slowest optimization algorithm.
quotes: To showcase the scalability of our approach we evaluate our method on large 50 qubit, 2000 gate circuits.
We find [27] and our method to be the strongest CNOT optimizers compared to both pyzx and
While our method performs best in both the random and assembled random circuits, we have to note that it is also the slowest optimization algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the authors note the comparison is not completely unbiased.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results are a first step on small quantum circuits with a fixed number of gates, tested on four or five-qubit circuits with eighty gates per circuit, and that the agent did not have access to the complete set of ZX transformations.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-E end and Section V Future work
quotes: These initial results are promising, yet they represent only the first step in our research, where we study the effectiveness of our method for small quantum circuits and a fixed number of gates.
All the results presented here were tested on four or five-qubit circuits with eighty gates per circuit.
the agent did not have access to the complete set of transformations on the ZX diagrams.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated scope and limit, Section V.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum walk informed variational algorithm design
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, background start, theorem statements, benchmark section 8.4 (scheduling and portfolio set-up and results), Section 9 Discussion and Section 10 Conclusion. Sections 3 to 7 derivations and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A continuous-time quantum walk framework for analyzing mixing unitaries in quantum variational algorithms, with new QMOA and QWOA-CS algorithms benchmarked on parallel machine scheduling and portfolio rebalancing.

assertions.value: The authors report that for parallel machine scheduling the QMOA reaches the highest average approximation ratio at each ansatz depth, 0.973 at p = 5 for both Schedule A and Schedule B, against QAOA averages of 0.883 (Schedule A) and 0.942 (Schedule B).
quotes: The QMOA achieves the highest average at each ansatz depth, which, at p = 5, is 0.973 for both Schedule A and Schedule B.
The corresponding QAOA averages are 0.883 (Schedule A) and 0.942 (Schedule B).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result on two small problem instances.

assertions.value: The authors state that their numerical results indicate QWOA-CS can significantly outperform the original QWOA on portfolio rebalancing, and that for both scheduling and portfolio problems algorithms whose mixing graphs have lower MSV consistently achieved the highest approximation ratio and strongest amplification of the globally optimal solution.
quotes: Our numerical results indicate that the QWOA-CS can significantly outperform the original QWOA.
QVAs with mixing unitaries defined by graphs with lower MSV consistently achieved the highest approximation ratio and the strongest amplification of the globally optimal solution
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result on small instances in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that whether the exponential amplification scaling can be realised in practice depends on how well problems of interest can approximate the idealised phase distribution with a suitable choice of variational parameters, and that their numerical results come from a noise-free simulation.
quotes: Whether this scaling behaviour can be realised in practice depends on the extent to which problems of interest can approximate this idealised phase distribution with a suitable choice of variational parameters.
Numerical results were obtained using QuOp_MPI, which computes a noise-free simulation of the QVA phase-shift and mixing unitaries
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated limit and simulation set-up, Section 9 and Section 8.4.

papers.title_in_file: Trainable Quantum Spectral Models for Partial Differential Equations
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section II, most of Section III (architectures, benchmarks, dataset, training), Section IV results, Section V discussion, Section VI conclusion. Remaining architecture definitions (HHL-inspired and fully spectral details) read only in outline. Figure data not extractable.
papers.what_it_is: Variational quantum models that learn inverse differential operators in a spectral basis, compared with hardware-efficient ansatz circuits on Poisson and Helmholtz style PDEs in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that across Poisson, Helmholtz and variable-coefficient Poisson benchmarks, quantum spectral models produced more accurate spectral reconstructions and faster convergence than generic HEA circuits.
assertions.anchor: Section VI Conclusion; Section IV Results, Figures 3 to 6 (figure data not quoted)
quotes: Across Poisson, Helmholtz, and variable-coefficient Poisson benchmarks, QSMs produced more accurate spectral reconstructions and faster convergence than generic HEA circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study on small synthetic problems.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the richer spectral models, increasing circuit complexity beyond a threshold degrades convergence without improving accuracy, and that higher expressibility did not imply better performance.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section IV-F and Section V
quotes: Beyond this threshold, increased circuit complexity degrades convergence without improving accuracy.
Figure 8 shows that higher expressibility does not imply better performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors state that targets were built with only the first K = 7 of N = 16 modes carrying nonzero energy, that each experiment was repeated over 5 random seeds, and that some QSM architectures may admit efficient classical approximations because they restrict the trainable operator to structured subspaces.
assertions.anchor: Section III-C, III-D and Section V Discussion
quotes: In all experiments, the target solutions are constructed using a truncated spectral representation, where only the first K = 7 modes (out of N = 16 total modes) carry nonzero energy.
To assess robustness with respect to parameter initialization and stochastic effects, each experiment is repeated over 5 random seeds.
Finally, some QSM architectures may admit efficient classical approximations because they restrict the trainable operator to structured subspaces.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated set-up and limit, Sections III and V.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum-inspired anomaly detection, a QUBO formulation
papers.what_it_is: A QUBO formulation of anomaly detection solved with a classical QUBO solver (qbsolv) and benchmarked by ROC AUC against scikit-learn detectors on Gaussian, MNIST and credit card fraud data.

assertions.value: The author reports that the QUBO formulation of anomaly detection shows improved accuracy compared with classical methods on random data sets and real-world data sets, with each benchmark instance solved using qbsolv and scored by ROC AUC. The per-method scores are given only in figures.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.2 and Section 4 Conclusion, Figures 1 to 3 (scores only in figures)
quotes: In this article, I present a novel QUBO formulation for anomaly detection which shows improved accuracy in comparison with classical methods on random data sets as well as real-word data sets.
Each benchmark instance is solved using qbsolv, and the metric is the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC AUC) score.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one single-author study; scores only in figures.

assertions.value: The author states that the outlier selection penalty (equation 3) imposes all-to-all quadratic interactions, making the QUBO not solvable by near-term QPUs, and that the algorithm can instead be solved without hardware constraint using simulated quantum annealing, simulated annealing or any QUBO solver.
quotes: however the outlier selection penalty (equation 3) imposes all-to-all quadratic interactions, making the QUBO not solvable by near-term QPUs.

Nevertheless, this quantum-inspired anomaly detection algorithm can be solved without hardware constraint and with high number of variables using simulated quantum annealing, simulated annealing, or any QUBO solver.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own stated limit, Section 4 p.7.

assertions.value: The author states that the credit card fraud benchmark data set holds transactions from two days in September 2013 by european cardholders, with 492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions, a positive class of 0.172 percent of all transactions.
quotes: The data set contains credit card transactions that occured in two days in September 2013 by european cardholders, there are 492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions.
The data set is highly unbalanced, the positive class (frauds) account for 0.172 percent of all transactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors own description of the benchmark data set, Section 3.2.3.
